content: Uterine leiomyomas, also known as myomas or fibroids, are benign tumors that originate from the smooth muscle cells of the uterine myometrium. These are the most common pelvic tumors in women. The occurrence of leiomyosarcoma, a rare malignant tumor, during surgeries for presumed benign leiomyomas is estimated to be approximately 0.51 per 1000 procedures, or about 1 in 2000 cases. Treatment options for symptomatic uterine leiomyomas include medical therapies, surgical interventions, and radiologically-guided procedures. Laparoscopic myomectomy is considered the gold standard surgical approach for women who wish to preserve their fertility or retain their uterus. One limitation of laparoscopic surgery is the challenge of removing large tissue specimens from the abdominal cavity through the laparoscopic ports. To address this, the morcellation technique was developed, which involves breaking larger specimens into smaller pieces to facilitate their removal. However, intracorporeal power morcellation carries risks, such as the potential scattering of benign tissue fragments, which may lead to the spread of leiomyoma or endometriosis. In cases where malignancy is unsuspected, power morcellation can inadvertently disseminate malignant cells, potentially worsening the prognosis by upstaging the cancer. To mitigate these risks, a technique called in-bag morcellation has been introduced, where the tissue is morcellated within a containment bag to prevent the dissemination of tissue fragments. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of in-bag extracorporeal manual morcellation compared to uncontained intracorporeal power morcellation during laparoscopic myomectomy. A comprehensive search was conducted on July 1, 2019, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Specialized Register of Controlled Trials, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, LILACS, PubMed, Google Scholar, and two trial registries. Reference lists of retrieved articles were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted for additional or ongoing trials. The study included randomized controlled trials comparing in-bag extracorporeal manual morcellation with uncontained intracorporeal power morcellation in premenopausal women undergoing laparoscopic myomectomy. Standard Cochrane methods were followed for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed trial eligibility, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Data accuracy was verified, and summary measures were reported as risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Outcomes of interest included intraoperative and postoperative complications, operative times, ease of morcellation, length of hospital stay, postoperative pain, conversion to laparotomy, and postoperative diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma. Two trials involving 176 premenopausal women with fibroids were included. In the experimental group, in-bag manual morcellation was performed, where each enucleated myoma was placed into a specimen retrieval bag and manually morcellated using a scalpel or scissors. In the control group, uncontained intracorporeal power morcellation was used to reduce the size of the myomas. No intraoperative complications, such as accidental morcellation of the liver, conversion to laparotomy, endoscopic bag disruption, bowel injury, bleeding, or injury to any organ or vessel, were reported in either group in either trial. The evidence for total operative time was of very low quality and inconclusive (MD 9.93 minutes, 95% CI -1.35 to 21.20; 2 studies, 176 participants; I² = 35%). Similarly, the evidence for ease of morcellation was also of very low quality and inconclusive (MD -0.73 points, 95% CI -1.64 to 0.18; 1 study, 104 participants). The morcellation operative time was slightly longer in the in-bag manual morcellation group, but the evidence quality was very low (MD 2.59 minutes, 95% CI 0.45 to 4.72; 2 studies, 176 participants; I² = 0%). No postoperative diagnoses of leiomyosarcoma were reported in either group in either trial. The quality of the evidence was downgraded due to indirectness and imprecision, stemming from the limited number of trials conducted in high-income settings, small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and the low frequency of events. As a result, the findings are highly uncertain. In conclusion, there is limited evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of in-bag morcellation during laparoscopic myomectomy compared to uncontained power morcellation. The available data do not allow for definitive conclusions about the impact of in-bag morcellation on intraoperative complications, total operative time, or ease of morcellation. No cases of postoperative leiomyosarcoma were reported in either group. The two included trials were not adequately powered to detect rare outcomes, such as intraoperative complications or postoperative leiomyosarcoma diagnoses. Larger, well-designed, and rigorously conducted trials are necessary to provide more robust evidence on this topic.
